turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: So the one that I'm most passionate about is how we work with customers is very different in a super early stage bet versus to what you do in a very established product like Jira. So the first part is, how can we innovate in a way that doesn't fuck up existing customers? Jira, 120,000 customers, Atlassian, 300,000 customers. We can't just go in there, start experimenting, breaking a whole bunch of shit that millions of people experience and go, "What are you doing, Atlassian?" So what we needed is to create this area where we could experiment that's away from Jira while being inside Jira. (01:18:06): That part was a bit tough. It's possible to do. In fact, I came across an article from Ben Weiss. No, sorry, Noah Weiss, it's from many years ago now. Where he was basically talking about innovating in a successful material product and talked about three stages of incubate, iterate, integrate. And as part of that he gave the examples of Instagram, Twitter, and Foursquare. Where basically he was explaining, at the beginning, for example, Instagram was a feed that was chronological. And then the team started to experiment with a popular tab that was on the side that was not integrated into the core of the product that everyone uses. (01:18:47): They iterated on that for a while. That became the explore tab and then the explore tab became the main feed. The feed is not chronological anymore, it's based on your interests. And that part really resonated with me where I was like, "You know what? We're going to try to apply that to Jira, which is we're going to build it in Jira, but we're going to extract ourselves from a lot of the core components of the core base to rebuild the UX that would work for the audience we're going after." (01:19:17): Our audience is product managers. They have no patience for spinners, things need to be visual. They need to be able to quickly move things around to visualize the potential options they've got on their roadmaps and stuff like that. It needs to be snappy, it needs to get out of the way, but also something that they can feel proud to present to their stakeholders to have discussions around that. (01:19:39): It can be bogged down into the details. It can go to very, very deep [inaudible 01:19:43]. It needs to be an area, a space where you feel like you can breathe and have creative conversations. And Jira's UI was not exactly known for that. And in fact, most of the product managers I talked to were like, "I don't want to do this in Jira. It's too strict, there's too many workflows, it's owned by IT," yada, yada. And so we said, "That's fine. We're going to experiment with an experience that's going to be detached from Jira still on the same platform." (01:20:09): And that's what we did, basically. And so this concept of incubate by working on something on the site, iterate until you've got it right and then integrate it back into the main product is something I would definitely do again. We're currently in the middle of the integration phase for Jira product discovery.
turns.zh:
因此，我最热衷于探讨的是，在产品初期阶段与客户合作的方式，与在像Jira这样成熟产品中与客户互动的方式有很大不同。首先，我们要如何创新，同时又不影响现有客户的体验？Jira有12万名客户，Atlassian有30万名客户。我们不能贸然进去，开始试验，破坏数百万用户正在使用的功能，然后再问：“Atlassian，你在干什么？”因此，我们需要创建一个独立于Jira但又能在Jira平台内进行试验的区域。  

（01:18:06）：这部分有点难。但其实是可以做到的。事实上，我曾看到本·韦斯（Ben Weiss）的一篇文章。不，抱歉，是诺亚·韦斯（Noah Weiss）的文章，那是多年前的。他主要讨论如何在成功的物质产品中创新，并提到了孵化、迭代和整合这三个阶段。作为其中的一部分，他举了Instagram、Twitter和Foursquare的例子。基本上，Instagram最初是一个按时间顺序排列的信息流。后来，团队开始尝试在侧边栏添加一个热门标签，这个标签并未集成到核心产品中，而是作为独立模块进行迭代。  

（01:18:47）：他们对此进行了长时间的迭代。这个标签最终演变为探索标签，后来又成为主信息流。信息流不再按时间顺序排列，而是基于用户兴趣。这部分让我深有共鸣，我想：“知道吗？我们要把这个方法应用到Jira上，即在Jira内构建，但要从核心组件中抽离出来，重建一个符合目标用户需求的用户体验。”  

（01:19:17）：我们的用户是产品经理。他们没有耐心等待加载，界面必须直观。他们需要能快速移动元素，直观地展示路线图上的潜在选项等内容。界面要流畅，避免冗余，同时还能让他们自豪地向利益相关者展示并进行讨论。  

（01:19:39）：如果陷入细节就会很麻烦，可能陷入非常深的层级（01:19:43）。需要一个能让人自由呼吸、进行创造性对话的空间。而Jira的UI在这方面并不出色。事实上，大多数我接触过的产品经理都说：“我不想在Jira上做这件事。它太死板了，流程太多，由IT部门控制”，等等。所以我们决定：“没关系，我们要在同一平台上打造一个独立于Jira的体验进行试验。”  

（01:20:09）：这基本上就是我们做的。因此，孵化阶段在平台上进行试验，迭代直到完善，然后再整合回主产品，这种方法我肯定会再次应用。我们目前正处于这个过程中。
Jira产品发现集成阶段的中期阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the lesson there is don't force yourself to be a part of the broader product, initially. First, figure out what it could be if it's its own thing, and then eventually you can integrate?
turns.zh: 因此，经验教训是，初期不要强迫自己成为更大产品的一部分。首先，要弄清楚如果它是独立产品会是什么样子，然后再逐步进行整合。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: It depends who you're doing it for and the programs that they've got. Don't feel limited by your platform to answer the core things that are necessary for your product to work, basically. So if the platform is good enough for us, if the UX was good enough for the product managers, we would not have done that. And we would've had a hard time justifying it, but because it was not, we basically gave ourselves the stamp to be able to do it. So still in don't fuck existing customers, something I read from a site, from Reforge that talk about the Safety Funnel. (01:21:16): So they have this thing where the typical growth funnel goes from acquisition all the way to revenue and there's a whole bunch of different stages in between. Your goal is to maximize the number of people who go through this funnel successfully. (01:21:29): And I was trying to explain to people what we were trying to do with Jira Product Discovery, and I was struggling to put a name on it. And it was we're going to work with a few, small number of customers up until it's right for them and then we're going to expose it to progressively more people. And I know it's very common sense, but that's basically what we decided to do instead of the Atlassian way, which was more, "Hey, we measure our success based on..." For example, at that time, I think it was still before all those projects, "... monthly active users." If that was a measure of success, we would've been pushed very quickly to go and expose it to as many people as we could. We didn't want to do that because if they would have a bad experience, it would've been very hard to claim them back afterwards. (01:22:11): So someone in Reforge put the name on Safety Funnel. So the Safety Funnel is amazing. People don't understand that. You basically put a hard stop and you limit the number of people who had bad experiences. And you do that for a while, up until you can prove it's amazing and then you invite more people. So we did a lot of that. So we basically created that pocket away from Jira to reimagine what Jira could be for product managers. And we only exposed that to a very small number of customers at first. So that's don't fuck existing customers' first principle.
turns.zh:
这取决于你为谁开发产品，以及他们的现有程序。不要因为平台限制而局限于回答产品运作所必需的核心问题。所以如果平台对我们足够友好，用户体验对产品经理来说足够好，我们就不会这样做。我们很难为此找到合理的理由，但由于现实情况并非如此，我们基本上给自己开了绿灯来推进。因此，遵循"不伤害现有客户"的原则——这是我从Reforge网站上读到的关于"安全漏斗"（Safety Funnel）的观点。（01:21:16）：他们提出的典型增长漏斗模型从获取用户到产生收益，期间有多个阶段。你的目标是让尽可能多的用户成功通过这个漏斗。
（01:21:29）：我试图向人们解释我们在Jira产品探索中的策略，却难以找到合适的术语。我们的做法是，先与少数客户合作，直到产品对他们来说足够成熟，然后再逐步推广。虽然这听起来很常识，但这正是我们选择的路径，而非Atlassian的做法——后者更倾向于"根据月活跃用户数来衡量成功"。如果以此为衡量标准，我们很可能会急于尽快推广产品。但我们不愿这样做，因为如果用户体验不佳，之后就很难挽回他们。
（01:22:11）：Reforge将这种策略命名为"安全漏斗"。安全漏斗非常有效。人们往往不理解其原理。它通过设置严格的门槛，限制用户数量，直到产品表现出色后，再逐步扩大推广范围。我们正是这样做的。我们为产品经理打造了一个独立于Jira的专属空间，重新构想Jira可能的功能，并最初仅向少数客户开放。这就是"不伤害现有客户"的首要原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the reason that's important, just to put a point there, is the business will start to get upset if you're making many customers upset.
turns.zh: 强调这一点的重要性在于，如果你让大量用户不满，业务部门会开始不满。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: That would've been it if we had triggered an incident that brought down Jira for millions of users. And first time might have been okay. I mean, by the third time we would've been asked to pack up and go home, I think.
turns.zh: 如果我们触发了导致Jira数百万用户无法访问的故障，那后果将不堪设想。第一次或许还能接受，但第三次后，恐怕我们早就被要求卷铺盖走人了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the advice there is just limit how many people get exposed to your very early product, even if it's going to hurt your numbers. You don't want to cause people to be like, "What the hell are you doing over there, man? [inaudible 01:23:17]."
turns.zh: 明白了。所以建议是尽量减少让过多用户接触到你尚未完善的产品，哪怕这会影响你的数据表现。你可不想让用户觉得：“你到底在搞什么鬼啊，老兄？[01:23:17的背景音]。”

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: So [inaudible 01:23:17] your numbers is now the interesting one. So how do you frame success and how do you define metrics when your goal is basically to work with a small number of customers for a super long time? So that's what I ended up defining for this, is based on a term that was used at Atlassian that I tried to formalize it into something that everyone could refer to, which is the Lighthouse Users Program. And so the principle for it is it's a program, so it's an official thing. We have hundreds of thousands of customers at Atlassian, but we would only build the experience for a small number of them. And so there are stages to it. (01:23:56): The first stage is we work with 10 and we prove that the problems that they had are the things that we solved and where we spend most of the time for the first 10 Lighthouse Users is to explain why they are the Lighthouse Users. (01:24:13): Everything that explains why we believe they are a proxy for every customer that we serve afterwards. We then have this stage from 10 to 100 where we recruit more customers, but we're still not in the fully self-service, don't need a lot of onboarding stuff. We're still testing out the value, but we're testing the different variations in the scenarios that people face to make sure that the core solution that we've got can cater for those. So there's a lot of different options and different security needs. There's a lot of subtleties that you catch between 10 and 100. (01:24:44): Then we get to a stage where we're like, "You know what? It's good. It solves people's problems, but it's not self-service. We just need to explain stuff. We need to work with people on Slack. We need to work with them and answer a lot of support tickets or do a lot of Zoom calls to explain stuff." (01:24:58): Now we need to get from 100 to 1,000, and by getting there we basically need to solve all of that and after that we graduate. So basically by detailing that and explaining all the success criteria in between, it helps to define success in that in the make phase, we've got 10, 100, 1,000, and then people can understand exactly where we're at there, and the types of questions we're trying to answer. In the 10, we're answering every question with a user, snippet of a video call with them, either talking about their problem and solution but showing the product and how they solve with it. (01:25:34): That's how we wanted our stakeholders to view it, which is it's very qualitative, but have it felt from the user's perspective. It's different when we go from 10 to 100, from 100 to 1,000, but for each of those there's a playbook for how you go from one to the other. That helped us because we could then clean the space to do the right thing and we will not ask to hit, for example, a multi-active user's number or number of customers' number or percentage of users who use this number. Because it's very qualitative still when we're at that stage.
turns.zh:
好的，用户让我把一段英文翻译成中文。首先，我需要仔细阅读原文，理解其内容和结构。这段文字主要讲的是Atlassian的Lighthouse用户计划如何定义成功标准，以及在不同阶段如何衡量用户反馈和产品价值。

首先，处理专有名词和术语，比如“Lighthouse Users Program”应该翻译为“灯塔用户计划”，而“Atlassian”可以保留不译，或者根据上下文处理。这里可能需要保留原名，因为Atlassian是一个知名的公司名称。

接下来，注意句子的结构和逻辑关系。原文中有多个阶段描述，比如从10个用户到100个用户，再到1000个用户，每个阶段的目标和挑战都需要准确传达。例如，“prove that the problems they had are the things we solved”要翻译得自然，保持原意的同时符合中文表达习惯。

还要注意口语化和正式之间的平衡。原文中有一些口语化的表达，比如“So [inaudible 01:23:17] your numbers is now the interesting one.” 这里可能需要处理成更流畅的中文，同时保持口语化的感觉，比如“所以现在你们的数据变得很有意思了。”

另外，注意时间节点和步骤的连贯性。例如，“from 10 to 100”要明确翻译为“从10个用户到100个用户”，确保读者能清楚理解每个阶段的转换过程。

还有一些技术细节，比如“self-service”翻译为“自助服务”比较合适，而“support tickets”则是“支持工单”。需要确保这些术语在中文中有对应的标准译法。

最后，检查整体译文的流畅性和准确性，确保没有遗漏关键信息，同时保持专业性和口语化的平衡。例如，原文中的“playbook”可以翻译为“路线图”或“指南”，根据上下文选择最合适的词汇。

完成初稿后，再通读一遍，调整语序和用词，确保自然易懂。比如将长句拆分为短句，使用更符合中文习惯的连接词，让译文读起来顺畅自然。

总之，这个过程需要仔细理解原文，准确传达信息，同时保持语言的流畅和自然，确保最终译文既忠实于原意，又符合中文的表达习惯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool and super interesting. And it's along the lines of the gates. It aligns with, at each gate, here's how many users we're looking for. Basically, it sets expectations for what success is, keeps you from having to scale things too early. It's such a cool idea. And you call it Lighthouse Users, like the Lighthouse Users Program?
turns.zh: 太酷了，太有意思了。这和网关的理念很相似。每个网关对应的需求都清晰明了。本质上，它设定了成功的标准，避免过早地扩展规模。这真是个绝妙的创意。你们把它叫做“灯塔用户计划”吗？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Lighthouse Users, and there's two sides to it. We just talked about the stakeholder facing side. The one I love is the team facing side of this, which is I've seen a lot of teams, Atlassian and other companies as the products grow, you tend to leverage a lot more user research, formal user research or CSAT service. And the way I call it, it's hiding behind research and not being close enough to the ground with customers. And what I want to do in the teams I work with is to create a direct feedback loop with customers, but not like someone gives you feedback and you do it. We talk...
turns.zh: “灯塔用户计划”分为两部分。我们刚刚讨论了面向利益相关者的方面。我更关注的是面向团队的部分。在Atlassian和其他公司，随着产品规模的扩大，大多数团队往往会过度依赖用户研究、正式的用户调研或客户满意度评分（CSAT）等工具。但在我看来，很多团队会躲在调研数据背后，却与客户严重脱节。我希望在合作的团队中建立与客户的直接反馈机制，不是那种“听取反馈然后照做”的模式，而是要真正与客户对话、为他们开发产品。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: ... with customers, but not like someone gives you feedback and you do it. We talk to those customers, we build stuff for them. So there's something I've seen which is climate change. It's a thing. Everyone knows it's a thing. We all read reports about it. We're all like ... Every time we read an IPCC report we're like, "Shit." Do we change anything? Not enough. (01:27:23): What makes people want to change and actually gives them a trigger to change? I've seen is a lot more empathizing with individual people's experience. If I know someone that's impacted by climate change, it's going to make me relate a lot more strongly to the concept of climate change and want to change myself. Sorry for the power note here. I'm-
turns.zh: ……不是那种“听取反馈然后照做”的模式，而是要真正与客户对话、为他们开发产品。我曾观察到一个现象，比如气候变化问题。每个人都知道气候变化是个大问题，我们都读过相关报告，但每次看到IPCC报告时，大家都会感叹：“天哪！”但真正促使人们行动的因素是什么？我发现，最有效的办法是深入理解个体用户的体验。如果我认识一个受气候变化影响的人，我会更深刻地感受到气候变化的严峻性，也更有动力去改变自己。对此我深有体会——抱歉，插句话了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, that's such a good example. Such a good way of making that point very clear of just the power of talking to a small number of users versus thinking that the more data you have, looking at data, CSAT scores, NPS retention will tell you what you need.
turns.zh: 没关系，你举的这个例子太贴切了。这充分说明了与少数用户对话的力量，比起依赖海量数据、CSAT评分或用户留存率，要有效得多。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: So what we do with that is we recruit 10 people and we put these people in front of the whole team, not just the PMs, PM, designer, engineering. We meet on Zoom, we chat, we work with the same ones over months to build a product. They are with us on Slack. We have regular things. (01:28:20): What we've seen, what I've seen going fast is that the engineers would go into a planning meeting and the PM would say, "So we should work on X," and the engineer will go, "Wait a minute. We've had a talk with this customer and they struggle with this so I think we should work on that instead and fix that part of the experience," and so on and so forth. (01:28:35): So all of a sudden you're not talking about a product manager, you're talking about a product team with product engineers. So there was this thing at Atlassian where we called some engineers were more like system engineers, some were more product engineers. (01:28:49): In my opinion everyone can be a product engineer. They just need to be exposed to the right user context. The right user context, what is it? It's 10 customers you know by name, you know their context, you know their problems. You can empathize with it. This empathy makes you want to act to change your product to solve their problem and you get really huge pride coming back out of it. (01:29:11): It can seem counterintuitive in a company like Atlassian. 300,000 customers, right? We should build for them. Well, you can't, right? We're limited in our ability to make changes that will work for the vast majority so might as well embrace that. Embrace that we are indeed biased, that we are indeed reacting based on feelings, like wanting to help or not wanting to help or reacting strongly to what you've seen, but we are embracing that to try and build the best product possible. I've actually seen that the outcome is, so far on this product it's worked.
turns.zh: 接下来我们要做的是招募10个人，并让他们与整个团队见面——不只是产品经理、设计师和工程师。我们通过Zoom开会、交流，几个月来与这些人共同开发产品。他们会加入我们的Slack群组，定期参与活动。（01:28:20）：我们观察到，进展迅速的关键在于，工程师们在规划会议上听到产品经理说“我们应该着手X项目”时，会反问：“等一下。我们和这位客户交流过，他们在某个环节遇到了问题，所以我认为我们应该先解决那个体验再说。”诸如此类的情况层出不穷。（01:28:35）：突然间，你讨论的对象不再是产品经理，而是由产品工程师组成的产品团队。在Atlassian，我们曾区分一些工程师，他们有的更偏向系统工程师，有的则更像产品工程师。（01:28:49）：在我看来，每个人都能成为产品工程师。他们只需要接触正确的用户情境。正确的用户情境是什么？就是10位你能叫得出名字的客户，你了解他们的背景、他们的痛点，你能感同身受。这种共情会促使你想要改变产品以解决他们的问题，进而收获巨大的成就感。（01:29:11）：这在Atlassian这样的公司里可能看似违反直觉。毕竟我们有30万客户，对吧？我们应该为他们开发产品。但其实做不到，对吧？我们无法为绝大多数用户做出通用改进，所以不妨接受这一点。接受我们确实存在偏见，确实会基于情感做出反应——比如想帮助用户或不想帮助用户，或者对所见所闻产生强烈反应。但我们正欣然接受这些偏见，努力打造最出色的产品。我亲眼见证了这种方法的成效——到目前为止，这个产品确实取得了成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you actually think about this from the perspective of how would a startup approach this? This is exactly how a company that's just starting out would approach it. So it makes tons of sense to think of it this way. It's just people don't actually do this. It's hard to do. (01:30:04): This is a segue to a question I wanted to ask. So it took probably a long time for you to show real success, real progress, real like, "This is going to work." First of all how long was that period of just like, "This is probably not going to work too. Oh wow, maybe this is going to work"? And along the same lines, how does Atlassian slash ... What have you learned about how to protect this, Pixar people call it an ugly baby? When an idea is new they call this an ugly baby. People don't want it. It's just like, "Get rid of this thing." (01:30:36): Man, that sounds mean to say, but that's the way they talk about it. That's the term in creativity.
turns.zh: 如果你从初创公司的视角来思考这个问题呢？这正是初创公司会采取的做法。所以用这种思路来考虑问题再合理不过了。只是人们往往不会这样做，这很难做到。（01:30:04）：接下来我想问一个问题。你们花了很长时间才取得真正的成功、真正的进展，才真正确信“这事儿能成”。首先，那段“这可能行不通”的时间有多长？接着，“Atlassian如何……” 你们学到了哪些保护创意的经验？皮克斯的人把这个阶段称为“丑陋的婴儿期”。当一个新创意诞生时，他们称之为“丑陋的婴儿”。人们不想要它，只想说“把这东西扔掉”。（01:30:36）：天哪，这么说听起来很无情，但这就是他们谈论它的方式。这是创意领域的术语。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: That's a good one.
turns.zh: 这个说法不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you protect that because that's the biggest challenge I think a lot of companies have is just like, "It's been six months. No one wants this. We're going to kill it." How do you protect it? So how long did it take for it to show success and what have you learned about how to protect?
turns.zh: 你们是如何保护这个成果的？因为我认为很多公司面临的最大挑战就是，"已经六个月了，没人想要这个产品。我们要放弃了。"那该如何保护它呢？你们花了多长时间才看到成效，又从中学到了哪些保护措施？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. So basically, internal comms is everything there. The way I saw my job as, a large part as being very clear on where we were, on what we were learning on, how fast we were learning, how fast we were moving. Being super honest every step of the way, not try to make shit up and try to make it bigger than it is, more successful than it is. (01:31:18): On the contrary, be very clear about what we're testing, where we're testing it. Doing that with data, doing that with personal customer stories because we all can constantly relate to the heart and to the mind. So that's what I always try to weave into comms that I then send weekly. (01:31:36): So we've got this product internally called Atlas, which have a project on Atlas. People can subscribe to this project and then weekly you send a tweet-sized update about your project. I was using that as a platform to communicate internally about this product and there were actually hundreds of people who ended up subscribing to this thing. (01:31:54): Every week when we were at the stage where we were trying to get the first version out to customers it was a weekly demo of the product and everything that we built. Show the momentum as much as possible. I was even saving features for one week to the next just to ... When I knew we were going to be on vacation, for example, just to have something to show this train that keeps moving, it keeps moving. You don't want to get in front of it. (01:32:17): But then what I needed to do is to balance that out with all the customer side of things. So when we started to put it in front of customers then it was snippets from customer conversations. No one is going to read a research report that takes 30 minutes to read. Everyone is happy to watch a three-minute snippet with four customers talking about something. So I was using that a lot every week by posting those out there and then sharing them widely on Slack to go, "This is what we learned. This is what this customer is facing in terms of problem with Jira. This is how we're solving it. This is them talking about it," that kind of stuff. (01:32:48): So I was publishing that there and then sending that everywhere on Slack. Those kinds of things are what give people a sense of velocity and speed, and no one wants to fuck with a high-speed train. You don't get in front of it. That doesn't help and you're going to look bad by doing that. So basically that ended up buying us the time that we needed to get out of this, I don't know how you call it, the ugly baby phase.
turns.zh:
是的。所以内部沟通至关重要。在我看来，我的工作重点是清晰传达我们所处的阶段、正在学习的知识、学习的速度以及项目进展。每一步都要保持诚实，不夸大其词，不虚假宣传。（01:31:18）相反，要清晰说明我们正在测试什么、在哪里测试。利用数据和客户真实案例来传达信息，因为大家都能感同身受。所以这些内容都会融入我每周发送的内部通讯中。
（01:31:36）我们内部有个叫Atlas的产品项目。人们可以订阅这个项目，每周你会发送关于项目的推文大小的更新。我把它作为内部沟通平台，数百人最终订阅了这个项目。
（01:31:54）当我们要向客户推出首个版本时，每周的演示会展示所有构建的内容，尽可能展示项目的进展势头。比如，当我知道团队要休假时，我会把功能推迟到下周再展示，保持项目的持续推进势头，不让进度停滞。
（01:32:17）但同时，我需要平衡客户方面的需求。当我们开始向客户展示产品时，就用客户对话的片段。没人会读一篇30分钟的研究报告，但大家乐意观看三分钟的四位客户讨论Jira问题的视频。所以我每周都会发布这些内容，并在Slack上广泛分享，"这是我们学到的经验。这位客户在Jira中遇到的问题。我们是这样解决的"之类的内容。
（01:32:48）我会在内部发布这些内容，并在Slack上广泛分享。这些举措能让人们感受到项目的快速发展势头，没有人想去阻碍高速行驶的列车。阻碍它毫无益处，反而会让自己难堪。所以基本上，这些措施为我们争取了所需的时间，摆脱了所谓的"丑陋的婴儿阶段"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: An ugly baby phase.
turns.zh: 一个丑陋的婴儿阶段。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: So basically it helped us get out of this phase where we don't have anything to show for yet because what we're showing is based on the learnings we're trying to get and we're trying to do that with, "Here's some numbers, here's some demos, here's some user snippets." Doing that every week because people can consume bite-sized content every week. They just struggle with the stuff where you come in three, four months later and go, "This is what we have to show for."
turns.zh: 基本上，这帮助我们摆脱了那种暂时无所建树的阶段——因为我们展示的成果都是基于不断积累的经验得来的，而我们正是通过“给出一些数据、演示内容、用户反馈片段”来实现这一点的。每周都这样做，因为人们每周都能获取易于理解的内容。但当三四个月后你再回头时，人们往往会说：“我们现在能拿出什么成果呢？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. How long was that period before it got out of this ugly baby phase for you? When did people start to get like, "Oh wow, this might work"?
turns.zh: 好的。那在你们走出这个尴尬的初期阶段之前，经历了多长时间？什么时候人们开始觉得“哇，这或许能行”？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Honestly, we had something dogfooding within two months, in the hands of the first lighthouse user within five months. We iterated on the alpha for maybe six months. We then entered a beta that lasted close to a year. (01:34:06): So I think at every step of the way people could see us going somewhere, and I think initially they judged, not the outcome. They judged the team a lot more than the outcome. (01:34:22): So there's all this talk of founder market fit and I think really that's what you need to be teasing out, which is, is it the right thing, going after the right problems? Then if they can answer yes in ways that you haven't thought about asking consistently week over week, it's enough. I think that's where we were up until the stage where we were able to give something to customers, but the first lighthouse user was five months in. So it didn't even matter whether it looked good or not because people could see, "Okay, that's what ... Oh, there's something there," right? (01:34:51): So I'm not sure if there's one precise moment where it happened. However, there was this one moment where we were like, "Okay, that's it. We're ready to go GA." One of the founders, Mike went, "No, you're not. That thing is ugly. I do not want to look at it. It needs to level up with the rest of the Atlassian design standards. Our customers have expectations from us on that front. Your stuff is functional, but it's way too early." (01:35:19): So we went and fixed it. Took us two, three months and then we were okay to go. But yeah, no, because we had point A, because we had this expectation set that it would take a while to get there and because we were able to show progress every week, we basically didn't really feel that moment where we don't know what to do with this because it's too early.
turns.zh: 说实话，我们在两个月内就实现了内部测试，五个月内就让首位试用用户上手了。我们对原型版本迭代了大约六个月，随后进入了持续近一年的测试阶段。（01:34:06）：所以我认为在每一步，人们都能看到我们在朝着正确的方向前进。我觉得最初他们评判的不是结果，而是团队本身。（01:34:22）：所以现在大家都在谈论创始人与市场的契合度，我认为这才是你需要去探究的核心问题——即我们是否在追逐正确的问题？如果他们能以你从未想过的方式持续给出肯定的答案，那就足够了。我认为在我们能够为客户提供产品之前，创始人与市场的契合度至关重要，但首位试用用户是在五个月后才出现的。所以产品是否美观并不重要，因为人们能看到，“好吧，这就是……哦，这里有东西在做事”，对吧？（01:34:51）：所以我不确定是否有某个确切的时刻让情况发生转变。不过，有个时刻我们决定：“好吧，就这样了。我们准备好上线了。” 其中一位创始人迈克说：“不行，还不行。这个产品太丑了。我根本不想看它。它需要符合Atlassian的整体设计标准。我们的客户对此有期望。你的产品功能性没问题，但现在还太早。” （01:35:19）：于是我们去改进了。花了两三个月时间，最终才准备好上线。但确实，没有因为我们有A点，因为我们设定了需要时间才能达成目标的预期，也因为我们每周都能展示进展，所以我们基本没有经历那种因为太早而无从下手的阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This design improvement phase, what I'm visualizing is you're this pirate that is invited to a nice dinner and you have to start cleaning up. You have to start looking good and become inter-society. It makes a lot of sense. (01:35:54): Also, what you're describing makes me think again of this concept of, it's your job to keep the flame alive and help it spread within the organization. So you have this idea and you're just like, keep momentum going, keep the flame growing by sharing constant updates, sharing progress, make it very easy to consume with little snippets and videos. So there's a lot of great advice here. (01:36:13): So timeline-wise, interestingly what I'm hearing is it basically took a year from idea to alpha, something like that. Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 在这个设计改进阶段，我想象的是你扮演一个被邀请参加豪华晚宴的海盗，但你必须先开始清理现场，提升形象，融入社会圈。这听起来很合理。（01:35:54）：此外，你所描述的内容让我再次想到这样一个理念：你的职责是让火种持续燃烧，并助力它在组织内传播。所以当你有了这个想法后，你就需要保持势头，通过持续分享最新动态、汇报进展，让信息易于获取，用简短的片段和视频吸引受众。这里有很多宝贵的建议。（01:36:13）：时间线方面，据我了解，从构思到推出 alpha 版本大概需要一年时间，对吧？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Just like seven months ... No, five months to first alpha1 customer.
turns.zh: 差不多七个月……不，五个月就推出了首个 alpha1 版本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: We stayed in alpha for six months.
turns.zh: 我们在 alpha 阶段停留了六个月。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, got it. So through alpha about a year total. Many people are hearing this. On the one hand it would be like, "Of course, Atlassian has all these resources. They're going to spend a year on this idea that who knows is going to work out. It's so easy for them." (01:36:43): I imagine there was much pain and suffering and challenge along the way that happened that makes it not so easy. Is there something you could share by just the struggle to actually make this real just as a way to wrap up conversation, go back to therapy if there's anything you want to share?
turns.zh: 好的，我明白了。所以整个 alpha 阶段大概持续了一年。很多人都听说过这个案例。一方面，他们可能会想：“当然，Atlassian 拥有那么多资源。他们可以花一年时间在一个谁知道能否成功的想法上。对他们来说太容易了。” （01:36:43）：我能想象这过程中肯定有很多痛苦和挑战。能否分享一下在将这个想法变为现实过程中遇到的困难，作为对谈话的总结，如果你愿意的话？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. Basically, it's pretty much what we talked about earlier with lots of processes that were not changed yet because we're at the very beginning of point A, and people still wanting us to chime in on the things that were important for their part of the organization where we would play a part later if we become successful. (01:37:19): So none of that stuff was just solved once and for all. It was just a constant process to play with that, but I think we managed to get out of these things pretty gracefully in the end and I think we gained some level of admiration for some teams from that and some found it a bit ... It's always interesting to see someone breaking the rules and getting away with it. I think it inspired some of the other founders to try and do that, which was pretty cool to see. (01:37:46): It's actually something I'd love to see more, hearing back from the customers I've been talking to about this in their company, rather than feel suffocated by the current processes and they don't feel like they can break the chains. So I'm hoping it inspires a few more teams to give it a go, really.
turns.zh: 是的。基本上，正如我们之前讨论的，有很多流程还没有改变，因为我们还处于 A 点的最初阶段，人们仍然希望我们参与到对他们所在组织部门至关重要的事情中，而如果我们成功了，之后我们会参与进来。（01:37:19）：所以这些问题并没有一劳永逸地解决。这是一个持续调整的过程，但我认为我们最终还是比较顺利地克服了这些困难。通过这个过程，我们赢得了一些团队的赞赏，而有些团队则觉得有点……看到有人打破规则却能逃脱惩罚总是很有趣的。我认为这激励了其他一些创始人也去尝试这样做，这真的很棒。（01:37:46）：实际上，我很希望能看到更多这样的例子。从我接触过的客户那里了解到，他们在自己的公司里也面临着类似的困境，被现有流程压得喘不过气来，感觉无法突破束缚。所以我真心希望这能激励更多团队勇于尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's clearly more I want to learn about point A and how other companies do this incubation stuff. So this is a really good inspiration to dig deeper into those sorts of programs. (01:38:18): We've covered a lot of ground. We've talked about things that have worked and haven't worked, all kinds of therapy and pain, but also things that help you succeed and build amazing products. Is there anything else you want to share or leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 显然，我还想进一步了解A点，以及其他公司如何开展孵化项目。这确实给了我一个很好的启发，让我能更深入地研究这类项目。（01:38:18）：我们已经讨论了很多内容，包括哪些方法有效、哪些无效，各种治疗手段和应对挑战的方法，还有助力成功和打造卓越产品的要素。在我们迎来激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享或留给他们的吗？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. I would try to balance the point I just gave, which is it's hard so someone has to try. Always feel like you can push. I'd like to balance that a bit with be careful for yourself as well and make sure that you're doing this in an environment that's ready to welcome it. (01:38:54): So as I mentioned, I worked at Atlassian now for the past 10 years. Before that I used to work in banks, in heavily regulated industries, in a whole bunch of different areas where that kind of stuff was not okay. I could have tried to push, it would have not gone well at all. (01:39:15): So I think I'm deeply convinced by the fact that we don't need so much top-down leadership. What we need is a lot of autonomous leaders, regardless of their position within the org, able to push for change, fighting for the right things, but you need to do that in an environment that's safe for you to do so. If it's not, I think it's okay to consider alternatives. (01:39:37): So in other words, don't feel like you're trapped. Right? You only have one work life. Do it in places where you really believe you can do amazing work and surrounded by people that you're excited to work with. Otherwise, I've been there before where it's possible to become cynical by the weight of the things that are not possible and ending up doubting your own ability to do stuff really. So it's a bit of a balance of push for the right things, but also watch after yourself and if the environment is not right, it's okay to change.
turns.zh: 是的。我想平衡一下我刚才提到的观点，即成功需要勇于尝试。但也要提醒大家要保护好自己，确保所处的环境能为变革提供支持。（01:38:54）：正如我之前提到的，我在Atlassian工作了10年。在此之前，我曾在银行等受监管严格的行业工作，接触过各种不允许尝试新事物的领域。如果我当时强行推进，肯定会一败涂地。（01:39:15）：所以我深信，我们不需要太多自上而下的领导。我们需要的是大量能自主推动变革的领导者，无论其职位高低，只要能为正确的事业而奋斗，但前提是所处的环境要安全。如果不安全，那就该另觅良机了。（01:39:37）：换句话说，别觉得自己被困住了。人生只有一次。要在真正能发挥才能、与志同道合者共事的地方工作。否则，我深有体会——被各种不可能实现的任务压得喘不过气，最终怀疑自己的能力时，那种感觉实在令人心灰意冷。所以关键在于既要推动变革，又要自保。如果环境不合适，及时调整才是明智之举。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a really hot topic and common question in product management and I imagine other functions in product of just how much can actually change as an IC at a company. I hear all this advice about making change, changing culture, incubating stuff, innovating. How much can you actually make an impact versus, "Nothing's going to change. I should go work somewhere else"? Do you have any advice there? It sounds like basically you're saying there's oftentimes you have no impact on how the business and culture's going to work and you probably should go find a company like Atlassian that does learn how to incubate and innovate and think differently.
turns.zh: 这在产品管理领域是个热门话题，也是其他职能部门常面临的常见问题——即作为公司内部创新中心（IC）能真正带来多大变革。我听过很多关于推动变革、改变文化、孵化项目、创新等建议。但与此同时，又有人怀疑自己能否真正有所作为，认为“这里永远不会变，我还是去别处吧”。你对此有什么建议吗？听起来你基本上是在说，很多时候你对公司的运营和文化几乎无能为力，所以最好去找像Atlassian这样善于孵化和创新、思维开拓的公司。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. This one is a ... I'm not sure how to answer that really because I've worked with, consulted, worked for close to 50 companies. Atlassian is the first company I joined where I was at home from day one, challenged in the right way, but fuck, I can really choose my battles and go after them. Things are hard, but it's okay. (01:41:09): So I joined Atlassian. [inaudible 01:41:13] found the trampoline like that, but yeah, I would just go, not settle for status quo because you cannot be the only sane person in a room. At some point you will go insane. The environment will permeate on you. You are not this entity that is absolutely permeable to everything that happens around you. Everything around you will affect you and will change you as a person. I really believe that. (01:41:36): So you need to surround yourself with people and environments that can help bring out the best in you, otherwise you can turn bad. I myself have been cynical in the past working in environments that were cynical and I then decided it's not me. I do not want it to be me. It was me back then. I do not want it to be me. (01:41:55): So yeah, that's my only advice, which is have the courage to ask yourselves those questions because otherwise it might change you in ways you don't want to.
turns.zh: 是啊。这家公司……说实话我不太好回答，因为我曾与近50家公司合作过、提供过咨询服务、甚至在其中任职。Atlassian是我加入的第一家公司，从第一天起我就感觉如鱼得水，虽然面临挑战，但该死的，我真的能选择自己的战场并全力以赴。事情虽然艰难，但没关系。（01:41:09）所以我选择了Atlassian。[听不清 01:41:13]我就像那样找到了跳板，但没错，我会勇往直前，不满足于现状，因为你不可能成为房间里唯一理智的人。到某个时候，你也会变得疯狂。环境会对你产生潜移默化的影响。你不是那种对周围发生的一切都完全免疫的存在。周围的一切都会影响你，改变你这个人。这一点我深信不疑。（01:41:36）所以你需要让身边的人和环境帮助你发挥出最佳状态，否则你可能会变坏。我自己过去在消极的环境中工作时也曾心存愤世嫉俗，但后来我意识到那不是真正的我。我不想成为那样的人。我那时是，但现在不是了。（01:41:55）所以没错，这就是我唯一的建议：要有勇气问自己这些问题，不然它可能会以你不希望的方式改变你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing advice. Really important advice. With that we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒的建议了。真是至关重要的建议。好的，现在到了我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: I am, looking forward to it.
turns.zh: 我准备好了，很期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, here we go. First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。第一个问题，请推荐两到三本你最常向他人推荐的书籍？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah, the first one was a book that was recommended to me by Scott Farquhar, founder of Atlassian co-founder. Who: A Method for Hiring is basically a book about how to do the thing that I for a while was really bad at, which is try to interview to understand who's going to be a good person, not a good person to join your team. (01:42:44): Second one, so that's one book about work. Two other books that are not about work. Highly recommend reading Hakim's Odyssey. It's the story of a Syrian refugee moving out of Syria, trying to move into Europe. We hear a lot of these stats and numbers about people trying to cross the Med Sea or basically become refugees in other countries and it's very easy to look at it complacently up until you meet a personal story. This personal story of Hakim that was told very beautifully by this illustrator is well worth a read on that front. (01:43:19): The last one is a book that I'm not sure has been translated from French. It's called Vivre avec la Terre, To Live with the Earth and it's about how we could build a different agricultural system to the one that we have today that might have better ways to feed us into the future that doesn't require large monoculture of vegetables that may not be as sustainable. (01:43:47): They managed to create a really efficient structure on very small parcels of land with a lot of species working together to control and not need the use of any pesticides and stuff like that. They've been always surrounded by teams of researchers from the, I think it's called the Inria. It's one of the French research centers, have got really amazing results, but I don't think many know that this stuff exists and that it could actually be used out there and I think that's a shame.
turns.zh: 是的，第一本书是Atlassian联合创始人斯科特·法克哈尔推荐给我的。《谁：招聘方法论》这本书主要讲的是如何做一件事，而这件事我曾一度做得很糟糕——那就是通过面试来判断一个人是否适合加入你的团队，而不是判断他是否优秀。（01:42:44）第二本书讲的是工作。另外两本非工作相关的书籍。我强烈推荐《哈基姆的奥德赛》。这本书讲述了一位叙利亚难民逃离祖国、试图移居欧洲的历程。我们常听到诸多关于人们试图穿越地中海或成为他国难民的数据统计，但除非亲耳听过个人故事，否则很难对此产生切身共鸣。这位插画家生动讲述的哈基姆故事，绝对值得一读。（01:43:19）最后一本书我不确定是否有中文译本，书名叫《与地球共生》，探讨如何构建一个不同于现有农业体系的未来农业模式，通过更可持续的种植方式满足人类需求，而非依赖大规模单一作物种植。（01:43:47）他们在极小的土地上打造了高效农业体系，通过多种物种协同作用实现无农药种植，成果斐然。整个项目一直有法国国家信息与自动化研究所（Inria）的科研团队支持，成果惊人，但遗憾的是很多人并不知道这些技术的存在及其应用潜力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's the first book that sounds recommended that's only in a different language, but may not be translated.
turns.zh: 我觉得第一本书听起来不错，但可能只出过外文版，还没被翻译。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: It might be translated. I hope it is. It's pretty thick though and it's very technical. So I've read the principles bit and I would get lost in all the technical aspects of growing food, to be honest.
turns.zh: 或许有中文译本。希望如此。不过那本书很厚，内容很专业。我读过一些原理部分，但说实话，要是深入研究农业种植技术，我肯定会被淹没在各种专业术语中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, love it. So let's ask you your favorite interview question. What's your favorite interview question?
turns.zh: 好的，爱听。接下来问你最喜欢的面试问题。你最喜欢的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. So I struggled a lot with interviewing and I've read all the standard interview questions there is out there and I've heard them in your podcast as well. There is one that came from this book that Scott Farquhar also told me was working really well for him is when people describe an experience, you ask them the name of the person that they worked with back then. And you ask them, "So when I call this person after our call, what do you think they're going to say about that?" (01:45:02): Apparently this does something and I've seen it happen where people are unable to project and invent on the spot something from the lens of another person talking about them. So they might be able to talk about, "I did this, I did that, I did that. So when I talk ... "Who was your boss? My boss was ... So when I ask this person, what do you think they're going to say?" It's like, "Ah, well actually, I was only leading a part of it and maybe you shouldn't call them because XYZ." (01:45:33): That part makes people all of a sudden go out of this scripted version they give of themselves and become more real for a second. You get a bit of the authenticity coming out, which often is very hard to get to for me in interview questions. I've seen it happen. I find that very funny to do now because people get really uneasy for a second and then you get to something real.
turns.zh: 是啊。我在面试方面遇到了很多困难，我读遍了市面上所有常见的面试题目，甚至在你的播客里也听过不少。Scott Farquhar提到的一个方法特别有效：当求职者描述一段经历时，你可以问他们当时合作的同事的名字，然后反问：“那如果我打完电话后联系那个人，你觉得他们会怎么评价你？”（01:45:02）这种方法效果显著，因为人们无法即兴地从对方视角编造虚假经历。例如，求职者可能会说：“我做了这个、那个、那个。但如果你联系他们，他们可能会说……” 这时对方往往会坦白：“啊，其实我当时只负责其中一部分，或许你不该联系他们，因为……” （01:45:33）这种方法能让求职者瞬间脱离预设的回答，展现真实自我。这类真实的互动在面试中往往很难实现，但我亲眼见过它奏效，现在我觉得这招特别妙，因为求职者会瞬间变得紧张，但随后又能说出真心话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is genius. Makes so much sense. Makes me wonder how I can integrate this tip into my podcast interviews. Really good tip. Next question, do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 这招太妙了。太有道理了。让我好奇怎么能把这个技巧融入我的播客采访中。真是个好方法。下一个问题，你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah, it's got nothing with tech, nothing to do with tech. I'm kite surfing a lot at the moment and I came across hydrofoils, which is basically these things where there's an airplane underneath you on a mast which is connected to a board. You're on the board with your kite and you basically just fly over the water. (01:46:32): That invention is just brilliant. It's relatively easy to learn and I can spend basically, parts of my weekend flying over water in as much as a breeze of wind because there's absolutely zero friction between the board and the water. So that's, technically speaking I think is genius the way they created that and inspiring themselves from airplanes.
turns.zh: 有啊，不过和科技无关。我最近经常玩风筝冲浪，接触到了水翼板。这种装备的原理是板上有个气垫，连接着桅杆和冲浪板。你带着风筝站在板上，基本上只要有微风就能在水面上飞行。（01:46:32）这个发明太棒了。学起来相对容易，周末我就能在微风中享受水上飞行了。因为板和水之间完全没有摩擦。技术角度看，他们模仿飞机的设计真是天才之作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is that the thing that Zuck was riding with his sunscreen with the flag or is that something else? I don't know if you saw that photo. Don't worry about it.
turns.zh: 是扎克（Zuck）骑的那个带防晒霜和旗子的东西吗？我不知道你有没有看过那张照片。别在意。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: No, I didn't see that.
turns.zh: 没有，我没看到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that you say it's relatively easy to learn even though there's a kite on you pulling you in the water on this thing that's above the water. I don't know if I believe you.
turns.zh: 你说学起来相对容易，尽管板上还有风筝拉着你飞行。这我有点难以置信。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, there's sports and crafts that are difficult to learn. This one you can get comfortable in 18 months to two years, which is really, really short. It could be a sport that you would have done before.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，有些运动和手工艺很难学会。但自由潜水这项运动只需18个月到两年就能掌握，时间真的很短。可能你以前就参与过这项运动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a couple of years. Okay. I like your bar for ... I'm going to ask a question along these lines, but before we get there, do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, find useful in work or in life, maybe share with friends and family?
turns.zh: 就几年时间。好的。我喜欢你设定的标准……我接下来要问个相关问题，但在此之前，你有没有一条最喜欢的的人生格言，经常回味，在工作或生活中觉得很有用，或许还能和朋友家人分享？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: I've got two, one for work and one for everything in life. The one for work is initially a quote from Obama. I can't remember the exact quote. I'm going to paraphrase, but let's keep it about the work. So there's going to be moments in your career where you don't feel valued and you wonder, "Am I doing the right thing? Am I being recognized? Am I valued? Am I at the right place?" Whenever that happens, a lot of parasitic thoughts may come in. You may face imposter syndrome and stuff like that. Happens to me super regularly. (01:48:09): Whenever that happens, what I do is I remind myself, "Keep it about the work," because as long as you make it about the work there's always work to be done and there's always a path that emerges from that work. It's a bit of the same of this, you've got this thing in yoga where once you're committed good things will happen. Well, that's exactly what I've seen and that's helped me every time. I reread this quote whenever I'm in these moments of turmoil around me. (01:48:37): Now when I face those moments I also remind myself of the other one, which I invented, but I don't think I'm the only one who has invented that one, which is, "Remember that in 100 years we'll all be dead and forgotten. So don't take yourself too seriously. You're not that important. You're probably not that important, as important as you think for the people that you are arguing with." (01:49:01): That's also the beauty in all things, which is it has an end. In the end it probably doesn't matter so might as well give it your best shot. That's what the existentialists back in France many generations ago were talking about. This point is close to Albert Camus' thesis, right? "If it doesn't make sense might as well go for it."
turns.zh: 我有两条，一条用于工作，另一条适用于生活中的所有事情。工作方面的格言最初是奥巴马的一句话。我记不清具体内容了。我会意译一下，但还是围绕工作来说。当你职业生涯中遇到不被重视、怀疑自己是否做对了、是否被认可、是否在正确的地方等时刻时，很多消极想法可能会涌现。你可能会遭遇冒名顶替综合症之类的问题。我经常遇到这种情况。（01:48:09）：每当这种时候，我就会提醒自己，“专注于工作”，因为只要专注于工作，就总有事可做，总能从工作中找到出路。自由潜水也有个道理，一旦全身心投入，好的事情就会发生。这正是我每次陷入困境时都会重读的格言。（01:48:37）：面对这些时刻，我也会提醒自己另一条格言，也是我自己总结的，但我相信不止我一个人这么想：“记住，100年后我们都将死去，被遗忘。所以别太把自己当回事。其实你没那么重要。可能没你想象的那么重要，对与你争执的人来说也一样重要。”（01:49:01）：这也是万物存在的美丽之处——终有尽头。到头来或许都无关紧要，所以不妨全力以赴。这正是法国几代前存在主义者所说的观点，对吧？“如果这事没有意义，那就放手去做吧。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Really good points, really good lessons, really good mottos. Final question, you were ranked number four worldwide in a form of free diving. First of all, can you briefly describe what is free diving and then can you share one thing that might surprise someone about the sport and the skill?
turns.zh: 很棒的观点，很棒的教训，很棒的格言。最后一个问题，你在自由潜水项目中全球排名第四。首先，能简单描述一下自由潜水吗？然后分享一个关于这项运动和技能可能令人惊讶的点吗？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. So yes, that's my claim to fame. I was ranked number four in basically, the distance you can swim in a swimming pool without fins with 167 meters, which is 550 feet.
turns.zh: 是的。没错，这就是我的成名之举。基本上，我在泳池里不戴脚蹼游泳的最大距离排名第四，达到了167米，也就是550英尺。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And underwater?
turns.zh: 水下呢？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Underwater breaststroke. I went further with the monofin, the thing you see back there, but breaststroke was one meter away from the French record and ranking number four worldwide that year. The one I'm most proud of is I actually went to 300 feet underwater deep, came back in one piece and I really enjoyed the whole thing.
turns.zh: 水下蛙泳。我用脚蹼游得更远了，就是你们后面看到的那玩意儿，但那次蛙泳距离法国纪录还差一米，而且在那年全球排名第四。我最引以为傲的是，我实际下潜到300英尺深处，又安然无恙地浮上来了，整个过程我乐在其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 300 feet. That's like-
turns.zh: 300英尺。相当于——

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: 92 meters.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, geez. I'm trying to imagine what that is like compared to a Statue of Liberty or something like that, but I'll look that up later.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。我试着想象这和自由女神像之类的比起来有多高，但我稍后会查一下。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: I look at buildings one. Buildings can be as little as 20, 30 meters and can go super higher, but 90 meters is pretty high, yeah. Last time I looked at a building like that, I can't remember which one it was, but it's pretty high. So it's take one breath, go down, touch the bottom plate on the rope and then come back up. (01:50:54): One thing that may surprise people with this is that everyone is much more gifted at it than they think. So I used to give courses on the weekend for free diving and most people when I ask them, "Hey, how long do you think you can be underwater?" And they tell me something like 30 seconds, maybe a minute. "How deep you think can you go? Ah, maybe five meters." (01:51:15): At the end of the weekend most people were able to hold their breath for two to three minutes and to go to 20 meters deep. So it's one of those things where it looks absolutely impressive and crazy and amazing and in fact we're naturally gifted to it. There's a lot of physiological changes that happen when we dive that make it possible, but I think it's fascinating how little we know about our bodies.
turns.zh: 我先看看建筑物。建筑物的高度可能低至20、30米，也可能高得多，但90米已经很高了。上次我看过一栋这样的建筑，我不记得是哪栋了，但确实很高。所以是深呼吸一次，下潜，触碰到绳子的底部，然后再浮上来。 （01:50:54）：关于这件事可能会让人们惊讶的是，人们在这方面的天赋远超他们的想象。所以我过去周末免费教授自由潜水课程，大多数人当我问他们：“嘿，你觉得自己能在水下待多久？”他们会说30秒，也许一分钟。“你觉得自己能下潜多深？啊，也许五米。”（01:51:15）：周末结束时，大多数人都能屏息两到三分钟，并下潜到20米深处。所以这件事看起来绝对令人惊叹、疯狂又神奇，事实上，我们天生就具备这样的能力。当我们潜水时，体内会发生许多生理变化，使这一切成为可能，但我认为我们对自己身体的了解实在太少了，这很令人着迷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm looking up what is 300 feet compared to real-life objects on perplexity. So what is 300 feet compared to real-life objects? Here we go, 300 feet. The length of a football field. Okay, yeah. I should have realized that. Close to the length of a Boeing 737.
turns.zh: 我在perplexity上查了一下300英尺和现实物体的对比。那么300英尺和现实物体相比呢？来吧，300英尺。一个足球场的长度。好吧，是啊。我应该早点意识到这一点。接近一架波音737的机身长度。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. You need to look at it this way to get some perspective.
turns.zh: 是啊。你需要这样看才能有一些概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and a football field-
turns.zh: 是啊，而一个足球场——

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: You go underwater in that-
turns.zh: 你在水下潜入——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... Jesus Christ. Oh, my God. But I love your advice that people can do much better at the skill than they think.
turns.zh: 天哪。哦，我的天哪。不过我真的很欣赏你的建议——人们在某项技能上的表现往往比自己想象的要出色得多。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah. Everyone from kids to adults are really amazing at it actually.
turns.zh: 是啊。从孩子到成年人，每个人在这方面其实都相当了不起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tanguy, we've covered so much ground. I think this is going to help a lot of people that are trying to get better at free diving, but also at building zero to one within large companies. I am so thankful that you made time for this and that you shared some into this real talk and as you called it, therapy. (01:52:37): Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, maybe follow up on some of the stuff you talked about and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 坦吉，我们已经探讨了这么多内容。我觉得这对那些想提高自由潜水技能的人，以及那些想在大公司从零到一打造新业务的人来说，都会有很大帮助。非常感谢你抽出时间参与这次对话，也感谢你分享这些真知灼见和所谓的“心理疗法”。（01:52:37）：最后两个问题。听众如果想联系你，可以在哪里找到你？比如追踪你提到的某些内容，或者听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Yeah, so you can find me on LinkedIn if you know how to ... You don't need to know how to pronounce my name. You just need to know how to write it. I'm not super active on social media to be honest. I'm very much in the trenches building this product so I don't do much in terms of networking to be fair, but if you are using this product for example, and you have ideas for how we can improve it for you or you'd like to share some stories about how that's helped you or how it's not helping you, I'd love to connect because I spend a large part of my days talking to users, responding to support tickets and stuff like that. So, yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，你可以在领英上找到我，只要知道怎么操作……其实你不需要知道怎么念我的名字，只要知道怎么写就行。我说实话，在社交媒体上不太活跃。我现在主要专注于产品开发，所以没怎么搞社交，但如果你在使用我们的产品，有改进建议，或者想分享使用心得，我很乐意交流，因为我每天大部分时间都在和用户沟通，回复支持请求之类的。所以，嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Tanguy, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。坦吉，非常感谢你今天的分享。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. Honestly, it's been amazing and I hope some of my gibberish is useful to people.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。说实话，这次交流太棒了，希望我的这些碎碎念能对大家有所帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Definitely not gibberish. I think it's going to help a lot of people. With that, I'll let you go. Bye, everyone.
turns.zh: 绝对不是碎碎念。我觉得这些内容会对很多人有帮助。就到这里吧，再见各位。

turns.speaker: Tanguy Crusson
turns.en: Bye-bye.
turns.zh: 拜拜。
